title: Quantifying and Narrowing the Yield Gap of Taro (Colocasia esculenta L., Schott) in Samoa Using a Biophysical Crop Model
content: Taro is the world fourth most important root crop and a staple crop in Samoa contributing significantly to food and nutrition security. However, taro yield in Samoa remains below its potential, with a considerable yield gap.  In this study, the Decision Support System for Agrotechnology Transfer (DSSAT) was used to (1) assess the yield gap of the widely grown ‘Samoa 2’ taro variety under both dryland and wetland conditions, (2) examine the main factors associated with the yield gap, and (3) assess management practices that could narrow yield gap. Farmers achieved 7.22 Mg fm/ha in the dryland and 10.17 Mg fm/ha in the wetland, while the simulated attainable yields were 13.75 and 12.67 Mg fm/ha, respectively. Potential yields exceeded 30 Mg fm/ha in both systems. The total yield gaps were 23.81 Mg fm/ha (77%) in the dryland and 20.33 Mg fm/ha (67%) in the wetland. Observed constraints included the incidence of pests, diseases, and weeds, while DSSAT simulations identified nitrogen leaching, high rainfall, and periodic water stress as key factors limiting nitrogen availability, leaf area index (LAI), and biomass accumulation and partitioning. Simulated management scenarios combining optimized planting time, increased plant density, supplemental irrigation, and nitrogen fertilization substantially improved yields. The best-performing combination of 2 plants/m², 70 mm irrigation, and 300 kg N/ha achieved 30.39 Mg fm/ha in the dryland and 29.52 Mg fm/ha in the wetland, corresponding to yield gap closures of 97.3% and 95.2%, respectively.
